title: Build a Web Page: HTML and CSS
summary: Learn to build and style a simple web page that works well on a phone, using HTML, CSS and flexbox. All you need is a browser.
audience: Beginners aged 14 and up. No prior coding needed. A phone, tablet or computer with a browser is enough

lessons.title: How a web page is built: HTML structure

body.p: Every web page you have ever opened is a text file written in HTML, which stands for HyperText Markup Language. HTML does not calculate or make decisions. It describes what is on the page: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is a picture. The browser reads the file and draws the page. You do not need to install anything for this course. On a phone, tablet or computer, open any free online HTML editor in your browser, type the examples, and watch the result appear beside your code.

HTML is written with tags in angle brackets. Most elements have an opening tag and a closing tag with a slash, and the content sits between them. An element is the whole thing: opening tag, content and closing tag. Some tags carry extra information called attributes, written as name="value" inside the opening tag.

body.code:
Welcome to our school club.

About us

body.p: In the first line, p is the element name and Welcome to our school club. is its content. In the second line, href is an attribute that says where the link goes, and About us is the text the visitor sees and taps.
A complete page always has the same outer shape. Learn it once and you can reuse it for every page you make.

body.code:
Lagos Maths Club

We meet every Friday after school.

list: <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser to use modern HTML. It comes first.
<html lang="en"> wraps everything. The lang attribute states the language of the page, which helps screen readers and translation tools.
<head> holds information about the page that is not drawn on the screen: the character set, the viewport setting you will meet in lesson 6, and the title.
<title> is the text shown in the browser tab and in saved bookmarks. It is not shown inside the page itself.
<body> holds everything the visitor actually sees.

body.p: Notice the indentation. The browser ignores it, but it helps you see which tags sit inside which. Every tag you open must be closed in the reverse order you opened it: if you open html, then body, then p, you close p, then body, then html. Tags inside other tags are called nested. A few elements, such as meta and img, have no content and no closing tag.

check.q: Which element goes inside <head> and sets the text on the browser tab rather than on the page?
check.e: The head holds information about the page. names the tab; <h1> and <p> are visible content in the body.

body.p: Headings run from h1 to h6. Use h1 once for the main title, then h2 for major sections and h3 for parts of a section. Choose headings by meaning, not by how big they look; you will control size with CSS later. Paragraphs use p. Browsers collapse extra spaces and blank lines, so pressing Enter five times inside a paragraph does not create five line breaks.

body.code:
Accra Football Fans

Match days

Games are on Saturday.

Bring a drink
and a good mood.

body.p: The br tag forces a line break inside a paragraph. It is used rarely; most spacing is better handled with CSS.

check.q: How many <h1> headings should a normal page have?
o: As many as possible, for bigger text
check.e: Headings describe the outline of the page. Use one <h1>, then <h2> and <h3> for sections. Use CSS, not headings, to change size.

body.tip: Save your file with the ending .html, for example index.html. The name index.html is the usual name for the first page of a site. If your page looks wrong, check first that every opening tag has its closing tag.

body.p: A page of plain paragraphs is not much use. The web is called a web because pages link to each other, and people expect pictures and tidy lists. This lesson adds the three elements you will use most.

The a element (anchor) makes a link. The href attribute holds the destination, and the text between the tags is what the visitor taps. A link can point to another website using a full address, or to another file in your own project using a relative path.

body.code:
Read the latest news.

Go to the contact page.

See the timetable.

body.p: The first link has a full address starting with https://. The second looks for contact.html in the same folder as the current page. The third looks inside a folder called pages. A common beginner mistake is writing src instead of href on a link, which gives a link that goes nowhere.

The img element shows a picture. It needs two attributes: src, the file name or path of the image, and alt, a short text description. Alt text is shown if the image fails to load (common on slow mobile data) and is read aloud by screen readers for blind learners. It has no closing tag.

If market.jpg is in the same folder as your HTML file, the picture appears. If you spell the file name differently, or forget that capital letters matter on many servers, you will see the alt text instead. That is a useful clue when debugging. Always write alt text that describes what the picture shows, not words like image or photo.

Use ul for an unordered list with bullet points, and ol for an ordered list where the sequence matters. Each item inside either one is an li element. Only li elements should sit directly inside ul or ol.

body.code:
Things to pack

  • Pen
  • Calculator
  • Water bottle

How to make tea

  1. Boil water.
  2. Add tea leaves.
  3. Wait three minutes.

body.p: The ol list numbers itself 1, 2, 3, so if you insert a step in the middle the numbers update automatically. You can place a whole ul inside an li to make a nested list, which is how menus with sub-items are built.

check.q: What is missing from this image?
o: An alt attribute describing the picture
check.e: alt text is read aloud by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load. img has no closing tag, and href belongs on links.

steps: Create a file named index.html using the skeleton from lesson 1.
Add an h1 with your name and a p that says where you live.
Add an h2 called My favourite foods and a ul with three li items.
Add an a element that links to a website you like.
Add an img with a src, an alt and a width. Save and refresh the preview.

check.q: Which element makes a numbered list?
check.e: <ol> is an ordered (numbered) list and <ul> uses bullets. Each item inside either one is an <li>.

body.tip: Attribute values go in quotation marks, and they must be straight quotes. On phones, the keyboard sometimes inserts curly quotes, which break the attribute. If a link or image stops working, retype the quotes.

lessons.title: Semantic elements: giving the page meaning

body.p: You could build a whole page using only div, a generic box with no meaning. It would look the same as a page built with meaningful elements, but it would be harder to maintain and much harder for screen readers, search engines and other programs to understand. Semantic elements are tags whose names describe their role. They do not change how the page looks by default; they change how well the page is understood.

list: header: introductory content at the top of the page or of a section, such as the school name and logo.
nav: a block of links used to move around the site, such as the main menu.
main: the central content of the page. Use it once per page.
section: a themed group of content that usually has its own heading.
article: a self-contained piece that makes sense alone, like a news story or a blog post.
aside: side content only loosely related to the main content, such as a tip box.
footer: closing content such as contact details and copyright.

body.p: Here is a small page for a Kenyan school science club. Read it from the top and notice how each name tells you what its content is.

body.code:
Nairobi Science Club

  • Home
  • Events

Upcoming events

Volcano experiment

Join us on Thursday in the lab.

Tip: wear old clothes for messy experiments.

Contact: club@example.com

body.p: Notice that a navigation menu is really a list of links, so a ul is nested inside nav. Semantic elements combine with the lists and links from lesson 2; they do not replace them.

When you add something to a page, ask what it is, not what it should look like. A group of links for moving around the site is nav. A story is article. A group of related paragraphs under a heading is section. Only when nothing fits should you use div, which groups content for styling, or span, which marks a piece of text inside a line.

body.code: The exam starts at 9:00 sharp.

check.q: Which element should hold the main menu of links across the site?
check.e: <nav> marks the main navigation, so screen readers and search engines can find it.

list: strong marks text of strong importance, usually shown bold.
em marks emphasis, usually shown in italics.
blockquote holds a longer quotation.
figure and figcaption wrap an image with its caption.

check.q: What is the main benefit of semantic elements like <header>, <main> and <article>?
o: They tell browsers, screen readers and search engines what each part of the page is
They make the page load colourful styles automatically
They are required, or the page will not display
check.e: A <div> would look the same, but semantic elements carry meaning that assistive technology and search engines use.

body.tip: Do not choose strong or em just to get bold or italic text. Choose them for meaning. If you only want a visual style, use CSS, which you start in the next lesson.

body.p: HTML says what things are. CSS, Cascading Style Sheets, says how they look: colours, fonts, spacing and layout. A CSS rule has a selector, which chooses which elements to style, and a block of declarations in curly brackets. Each declaration is a property, a colon, a value and a semicolon.

This rule says: every p element gets dark green text of size 18 pixels. CSS spells the word color the American way. Writing colour will do nothing, because the browser does not know that property and silently ignores it.

The tidy way is a separate file, for example style.css, connected inside the head of each page with a link element. The same file can style many pages, so one change updates the whole site. For quick practice in an online editor you can instead write rules between style tags in the head.

body.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My Page</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>

list: Element selector: p, h1, li. Matches every element of that name.
Class selector: .note. Matches every element with class="note". A class can be used on many elements, and one element can have several classes separated by spaces.
ID selector: #logo. Matches the single element with id="logo". An id must be unique on the page.
Descendant selector: nav a. A space means: any a that is somewhere inside a nav.

body.p: The dot before a class name and the hash before an id name are part of the selector, but they are not written in the HTML attribute. Study this pair.

body.code:
Cape Coast Reading Club

Books are free to borrow.

Open every day.

Home
Help

body.p: The h1 turns navy because of #logo. Only the first paragraph gets the pale yellow background, because only it has the class note. The Home link loses its underline because it is inside nav, but the Help link keeps its underline because it is outside nav.

Separate several selectors with commas to share a rule: h1, h2 { font-family: sans-serif; }. A pseudo-class adds a condition. The selector a:hover applies while a mouse pointer is over a link; on touch screens it may apply briefly while tapping.

check.q: Which elements does this rule style?
check.e: A dot selects by class. A # selects by id, and a plain name selects by tag.

body.p: If two rules set the same property on the same element, the browser must pick one. The more specific selector wins: an id beats a class, and a class beats a plain element name. If both selectors are equally specific, the rule written later in the file wins.

body.code:
p { color: black; }
.alert { color: red; }

body.p: A paragraph with class="alert" is red, even though the p rule matches it too, because a class is more specific than an element name.

check.q: Both rules target the same paragraphs. What colour is the text?
o: A mix of red and blue
check.e: When two rules are equally specific, the one that comes later wins. That is the cascade.
check.code:
p { color: blue; }
p { color: red; }

body.tip: If a style does not seem to work, check four things: the spelling of the property, the dot or hash on the selector, the semicolon on the previous line, and that the CSS file is linked in the head with the right file name.

lessons.title: Colours, fonts and the box model

body.p: Now you can choose elements, so let us make them look good. Three ideas cover most of the styling in beginner pages: colours, fonts, and the box model, which controls space.

CSS gives you three common ways to write a colour. You can use a named colour such as navy or tomato. You can use a hex code, a hash followed by six digits or letters, where the pairs stand for red, green and blue, so #000000 is black and #ffffff is white. Or you can use rgb with three numbers from 0 to 255. These two lines mean the same thing.

body.code:
h1 { color: #ff0000; }
h1 { color: rgb(255, 0, 0); }

body.p: Use color for text and background-color for the area behind. Always check contrast: pale grey text on a white background is hard to read, especially on a phone screen in bright sunlight. Dark text on a light background, or the reverse, is safest.

list: font-family lists fonts in order of preference. If the first is missing on the visitor's device, the browser tries the next. End with a generic family such as sans-serif or serif.
font-size sets the size. px is a fixed number of pixels. rem is relative to the root font size, which is usually 16px, so 1.1rem is about 17.6px and respects a user's chosen text size.
line-height sets spacing between lines. A unitless 1.5 means 1.5 times the font size and makes paragraphs easier to read.
text-align can be left, right, center or justify.

check.e: Hex colours go red, green, blue. FF is the maximum, so this is full red with no green or blue.

body.p: Every element is a rectangular box with four layers, from inside to outside: the content, then padding (space between content and border), then the border, then margin (space outside the border that pushes other elements away). Padding is inside the box, so the background colour fills it. Margin is outside, so the background does not fill it.

By default, width sets only the content width. The visible box is then 200 + 20 + 20 for padding + 5 + 5 for border = 250px wide, and the margin adds 10px of empty space on each side outside that. Many people find this confusing, so a very common fix is to tell the browser that width should include padding and border.

The star selector matches every element. With border-box, the same .card is exactly 200px wide, including its padding and border, and the content shrinks to fit. Padding and margin can also be set per side, for example padding-top: 8px, or in one line: margin: 10px 20px means 10px top and bottom, 20px left and right.

check.q: Without box-sizing: border-box, how wide is the visible box?
check.e: By default width is only the content: 200 + 10 + 10 padding + 2 + 2 border = 224px. With border-box it would be exactly 200px.

body.tip: To centre a block that has a width, set margin: 0 auto. The auto margins on left and right share the leftover space equally. Practise by giving the .card a width, then changing padding, border and margin one at a time to see each layer change.

lessons.title: Layout for phones: viewport, flexbox and media queries

body.p: Most people in the countries this course serves meet the web on a phone. A page that looks fine on a laptop can be tiny and unreadable on a small screen, so you must design for narrow screens first. Three tools solve most of the problem.

Without help, a phone browser assumes a page was built for a wide desktop screen. It lays the page out at a wide width and then shrinks everything to fit, so text becomes tiny. This line in the head tells the browser to use the real width of the device instead.

body.code: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

body.p: Put it in every page, right after the charset meta tag. It is the single most important line for mobile pages.
Avoid fixed widths that are bigger than a phone screen. These rules make pictures shrink to fit their container and stop them from stretching past it.

body.h: Flexbox: a row of items that adapts

body.p: Flexbox arranges the children of a container along a line. Set display: flex on the parent (the container), and its direct children (the items) line up in a row by default. The main axis is the direction of the row, and the cross axis is perpendicular to it.

body.code:
Maths
English
Biology

list: display: flex turns the container into a flex container.
flex-wrap: wrap lets items move to a new line when they do not fit, instead of squeezing.
gap adds space between items without margins.
justify-content positions items along the main axis, for example center, space-between or flex-start.
align-items positions items along the cross axis, for example center.
flex: 1 1 150px lets each card grow, shrink, and start from a preferred width of 150px.

body.p: On a wide screen the three cards sit in one row. On a phone about 360px wide, they wrap into fewer per line, with no extra code. Use flex-direction: column to stack items vertically instead.

check.q: What does flex-wrap: wrap do in a flex container?
o: Lets items move onto a new line when they do not fit
Wraps each item in a border
check.e: Without wrap, flex items squeeze onto one line. With wrap, they flow onto the next line on narrow screens.

body.p: A media query applies rules only when a condition is true. The usual method is mobile first: write the simple phone layout as the default, then add rules for wider screens.
On a screen narrower than 600px, the menu items stack. On a screen 600px or wider, they sit in a row. Resize the preview in your online editor, or turn your phone sideways, to see it change.

check.q: When do the rules inside this media query apply?
o: When the screen is 600px wide or narrower
When the screen is wider than 600px
Only when the page is printed
check.e: max-width: 600px means "up to 600px", so these rules are for phones and other narrow screens.

body.tip: Test at a narrow width first. Check that there is no sideways scrolling, text is readable without zooming, and buttons and links are big enough to tap with a thumb.

quiz.q: A student opens her page and the browser tab shows the file name index.html instead of a page name. Which change fixes this?
options: Add a title element with the page name inside the head
Add an h1 element with the page name at the top of the body
Add lang="en" to the html tag so the browser shows the name
Add a meta charset tag naming the page, inside the head

quiz.q:
What is wrong with this code?

Welcome to Ace Club
options: The strong element is opened but never closed
A p element cannot contain any text, only other elements
Strong must be written in capital letters to take effect
The p element needs an href attribute to be valid

quiz.q: A link is written Contact but tapping it does nothing. What is the bug?
options: The destination should be in an href attribute, not src
The file name must start with https:// before it can open
The a element must contain an img element to be clickable
The word Contact must be a heading element to work as a link

quiz.q: Why should every img have an alt attribute with a useful description?
options: It appears or is read aloud when the image cannot be seen, e.g. on slow data or for blind users
It makes the image load faster, because the browser can skip downloading the picture file
It sets the width and height of the image, so the page layout does not shift
It is the file name the browser looks for when it searches the server for the picture

quiz.q: A recipe has four steps that must be done in order. Which markup is most suitable?
options: An ol containing four li elements
A ul containing four li elements
Four h2 headings
Four li elements directly inside the body

quiz.q: You are building a school website and want to mark the group of links that moves visitors between pages. Which element is the best choice?
options: div
nav
aside
article

quiz.q:
This HTML and CSS are used together.

Hello

.intro { color: red; } What colour is the text?
options: Red, because the rule .intro matches the paragraph with that name
Red, because browsers treat id and class names as interchangeable
The default colour, because a class selector does not match an id attribute
The text is hidden, because a rule that matches nothing hides the element

quiz.q:
Given p { color: black; } and .alert { color: red; }, what colour is

Warning

?
options: Black, because the p rule is written first and the first rule wins
Black, because every paragraph keeps its own colour from p rules
No colour, because two matching rules clash and cancel each other
Red, because a class is more specific than an element selector

quiz.q: A student writes p { colour: blue; } and the paragraph text does not change. What is the problem?
options: Blue is not a valid colour name in CSS
The correct property is spelled color
The p selector needs a dot in front of it
Each declaration must end with a comma

quiz.q: A box has width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid green; and no box-sizing rule. How wide is the visible box, not counting margins?
options: 200px
210px
240px
250px

quiz.q: A heading looks too close to the paragraph above it, and you want more empty space outside its border, not inside. Which property should you increase?
options: padding
line-height
margin
border-radius
A, B and C stacked on separate lines
A, B and C side by side in one row
Only A is shown; B and C are clipped away
A, B and C in a row, hidden until tapped

quiz.q: A flex container has display: flex; and justify-content: center; and the default direction. Where do the items appear?
options: Centred along the row, in the middle horizontally
At the very bottom of the container, in a vertical stack
Stretched into a single column down the left side
Hidden, because center needs a number such as 50%

quiz.q: A page has no viewport meta tag and looks tiny on a phone with a very small font. What is the best fix?
options: Increase every font-size to 40px so that the text is large enough on the phone
Delete the CSS file, because the stylesheet forces the page to shrink on phones
Add the meta viewport tag with width=device-width, initial-scale=1 in the head
Change the title element in the head so the phone recognises the page as mobile

quiz.q: A menu uses flex-direction: column by default and this rule: @media (min-width: 600px) { .menu { flex-direction: row; } }. How does it look on a phone 400px wide?
options: In a row, because media queries apply on every screen size
Hidden, because the screen is narrower than 600px
Broken, because min-width cannot be used with flex layouts
Stacked in a column, because the condition is false
